Unlike every other block this is DEVICE MMIO, not a CSR: the plugin drains the whole window with `qemu_plugin_read_memory_hwaddr` (physical address `l2c_base`, default 0xE0500000), and `ResumeDriver::restore_l2c` writes back ONLY the writable boot-static config registers -- Control (0x0008: `CEN` enable + prefetch + ECC + RAM timing), HPM Control (0x0010), Way Allocation Masks (0x0300..0x0328) -- via Program-Buffer word stores (`sw`, per DS220 11.8.3's <8-byte access rule). The read-only Configuration Register, the side-effecting CCTL command registers (writing one re-issues an L2 cache op), and the W1C error registers are captured but never restored. `StateDrain::drain_l2c` re-reads the config registers (`lwu`) for `--verify` (`state_diff` compares `l2c.ctrl` with the RO INITSTATUS[14] bit masked). This is the MMIO analog of the `mcache_ctl` (L1-enable) transport, and matters for the cycle figure the same way: an L2-enabled engine that resumed with L2 disabled would run the ROI severalfold slower. **Restore is HARD-gated on the engine having an L2C** (`Simulator::l2c_present()` from `_NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB > 0`): a store to an absent L2C region faults the Program Buffer, unlike a tolerant CSR write. Every current engine is built `NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB=0`, so the block is transported forward-looking and the restore/drain no-op today. QEMU seeds the L2C Control Register's reset value (`CEN=1`, DS220 11.8.7) at machine init (`andes_ae350.c`), so a guest that relies on the default is not drained as `CEN=0`.

ResumeDriver::restore_l2c writes back the writable boot-static L2C config
registers -- Control (0x0008: CEN enable + prefetch + ECC + RAM timing),
HPM Control (0x0010), Way Allocation Masks (0x0300..) -- as Program-Buffer
word stores (sw, per DS220 11.8.3's <8-byte access rule), staging address
and value in x5/x6 before the GPR loop overwrites them. The read-only
Configuration Register, the side-effecting CCTL command registers
(writing one re-issues an L2 cache op), and the W1C error registers are
never written back. StateDrain::drain_l2c is the dual: lwu (zero-extend)
read-backs of the same registers so --verify compares round-tripped
values instead of the stale QEMU1 passthrough.

Both are HARD-gated on the engine actually having an L2C (set_l2c,
wired from _NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB / _NDS_L2C_REG_BASE -- not the
cluster's has_shared_cache, which also covers L3 on ax46/ax66): unlike
a tolerant CSR write, a PB store to an absent L2C region faults. Every
current engine is built without an L2C, so this is transported
forward-looking and no-ops today.

New encoders encode_sw / encode_lwu (golden hex from riscv64-elf-as)
join the PB toolkit; new recording-bus tests cover the store/read-back
sequences and both gates (flag clear, engine absent).

好,總共 10 類問題,我們都碰過或討論過:

| # | 問題 | 例子 | 解法(現況) |
|---|------|------|------------|
| 1 | **Reset 預設值不一致**:程式沒寫過的暫存器,drain 到的只是 QEMU 的 default,不是 engine 的 reset | L2C `CEN`(QEMU RAM stub=0,HW reset=1);`msp_bound`(QEMU all-ones,RTL 0) | spec/IP 級常數 → QEMU seed(CEN=1);engine 級差異 → v6 write-mask |
| 2 | **wire 只帶值、不帶寫入歷史**:「沒寫過」和「刻意寫入等於 default 的值」分不出來 | 程式寫 `mcache_ctl=0`(關 cache)vs 從沒碰過 | write-mask 在 source 記「事實」,不用 consumer 猜 |
| 3 | **Restore 安全性不同**:CSR 寫到不存在的是 tolerant no-op,MMIO store 到不存在的 region 會 fault Program Buffer | 對沒有 L2C 的 engine 發 `sw` 到 0xE0500008 → PB fault | CSR 用 tolerant write + caps;MMIO 硬 gate(`_NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB > 0` 才 restore) |
| 4 | **副作用暫存器不能寫回**:restore 不是「全部寫回去」 | L2C CCTL Command(寫了會重發 cache flush)、W1C error regs | 全 window capture,restore 只限 boot-static 白名單(Control/HPM/WayMask) |
| 5 | **硬體自走的值無法 verify**:functional 與 cycle 兩邊本來就不同步 | `mip` timer bit、`mcycle`、`mhpmcounter3-6`、`INITSTATUS[14]` | verify 排除清單 / bit 遮罩 |
| 6 | **存取規則不同**:每類暫存器有自己的合法傳輸方式 | L2C 規定 <8-byte access → 用 `sw`/`lwu` 不能 `sd`/`ld`;`vtype`/`vl` 只能經 `vsetvl` | 每類走專用路徑(PB word store、abstract 逐顆、Tier B) |
| 7 | **Engine 能力差異 + QEMU 必須 engine-agnostic**:不能把某顆 engine 的知識寫死進 QEMU | M-only engine 沒有 S-mode CSR、沒 HSP;未來新 engine | caps/manifest gate 放 consumer 端(probe「量測不建模」);driver 負責配對 `-cpu` |
| 8 | **WARL 釘死/合法化差異**:restore 寫了但沒生效 | `dcsr.prv` 在 M-only 被釘在 3;`mnvec` 被 RTL 鎖在 reset vector | 寫後 read-back 驗證(prv 錯就 abort 提示換 engine)或 verify 排除 |
| 9 | **QEMU phase 的讀取路徑失真**:guest 在 QEMU 上「讀」config 走了跟 engine 不同的分支,transport 修不了 | BSP 讀 `mmsc_cfg.PPMA` 決定要不要設 PMA | `-cpu` family 配對 + property(`vlen=512` 是先例);遇到再加 knob |
| 10 | **單邊根本沒有的 device**:vsim 沒 model 的 MMIO,ROI 碰了就 fault | PLIC、PIT、WDT... vsim memory map 沒有 | ROI 約定不碰;ROI 內只用雙邊都 model 的(UART2、SimControl) |

input.content:
# Hybrid State Transport: Problem Checklist (MMIO + CSR)

The 10 problem classes we must solve when transporting MMIO / CSR state
between QEMU (functional producer) and a vsim engine (cycle consumer),
each with one example and the current solution.

## 1. Reset default divergence

An untouched register drains the PRODUCER's default, not the engine's
reset value.

- Example: L2C `CEN` -- QEMU's RAM stub reads 0, real HW resets to 1.
  `msp_bound` -- QEMU resets all-ones, RTL resets 0.
- Solution: spec/IP-level constants -> seed QEMU (`CEN=1` at machine
  init). Engine-level differences -> v6 write-mask.

## 2. Wire carries values, not write history

"Never written" and "explicitly wrote the default value" look identical
in the drained file.

- Example: program writes `mcache_ctl=0` (disable caches) vs never
  touching it -- same drained bytes on a caches-off QEMU default.
- Solution: write-mask records the FACT at the source (translate-time
  CSR-write decode in the plugin); consumers never guess.

## 3. Restore safety differs: CSR tolerant vs MMIO faulting

A CSR write to an unimplemented CSR is a tolerant no-op (cmderr
cleared); a Program-Buffer store to an absent MMIO region FAULTS.

- Example: `sw` to 0xE0500008 on an engine built with
  `NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB=0` -> PB fault.
- Solution: CSRs use tolerant writes + caps gating; MMIO restore is
  HARD-gated on hardware presence (`Simulator::l2c_present()`).

## 4. Side-effecting registers must never be written back

Restore is not "write everything back".

- Example: L2C CCTL Command register -- writing it RE-ISSUES a cache
  flush/invalidate; W1C error registers clear state on write.
- Solution: capture the FULL window for the record; restore only the
  boot-static writable whitelist (Control, HPM Control, Way Masks).

## 5. Hardware-driven values cannot be verified

Functional and cycle clocks legitimately diverge.

- Example: `mip` timer bit, `mcycle`/`minstret`, `mhpmcounter3-6`,
  L2C `INITSTATUS[14]`.
- Solution: verify exclusion list / bit masks -- not transport bugs.

## 6. Access rules differ per register class

Each class has one legal transport method.

- Example: L2C requires <8-byte accesses (DS220 11.8.3) -> `sw`/`lwu`,
  never `sd`/`ld`; `vtype`/`vl` are only restorable via `vsetvl`
  (Tier B); CSR restore is one abstract command per CSR (a batched
  csrrw sweep cannot tolerate a mid-batch fault).
- Solution: dedicated path per class (PB word store, abstract per-CSR,
  vsetvl staging).

## 7. Engine capability variance; QEMU must stay engine-agnostic

Never bake one engine's knowledge into QEMU -- hybrid pairs QEMU with
DIFFERENT engines.

- Example: M-only `ax45mpv_premium` lacks S-mode CSRs and HSP; a future
  engine adds CLIC/Smstateen.
- Solution: caps/manifest gates live on the CONSUMER side (probe:
  "measure, don't model"); the driver owns the pairing (`-cpu
  andes-ax66`, `vlen=512`). QEMU keeps only spec constants.

## 8. WARL pinning / legalization divergence

A restore write may not take; the two sides may legalize differently.

- Example: `dcsr.prv` WARL-pinned to 3 on an M-only engine; `mnvec`
  held at the reset vector by the RTL.
- Solution: write-then-read-back verification (prv mismatch aborts with
  a pick-an-S/U-engine error) or verify exclusion.

## 9. QEMU-phase read-path infidelity

The guest READS config on QEMU and takes a branch; if QEMU's config
differs from the engine's, the wrong path already executed -- NO
transport policy can fix this.

- Example: BSP reads `mmsc_cfg.PPMA` to decide whether to program PMA.
- Solution: `-cpu` family pairing + per-knob properties (`vlen=512` is
  the precedent); add knobs as needed.

## 10. Devices that exist on only one side

MMIO regions vsim does not model fault when touched in the ROI.

- Example: PLIC, PIT, WDT, RTC, GPIO... absent from vsim's memory map.
- Solution: ROI contract -- do not touch them; inside the ROI use only
  dual-modeled devices (UART2, SimControl/HTIF).

## One-line summary

CSRs travel via "caps + write-mask + tolerant write"; MMIO travels via
"full-window capture + whitelist restore + hardware-presence gate";
verify masks hardware-driven values; engine knowledge stays in the
consumer/driver, QEMU keeps only spec constants.

# Hybrid State Transport: Problem Checklist (MMIO + CSR)

The 10 problem classes we must solve when transporting MMIO / CSR state
between QEMU (functional producer) and a vsim engine (cycle consumer),
each with one example and the current solution.

## 1. [MMIO + CSR] Reset default divergence

An untouched register drains the PRODUCER's default, not the engine's
reset value.

- Example: L2C `CEN` -- QEMU's RAM stub reads 0, real HW resets to 1.
  `msp_bound` -- QEMU resets all-ones, RTL resets 0.
- Solution: spec/IP-level constants -> seed QEMU (`CEN=1` at machine
  init). Engine-level differences -> v6 write-mask.

## 2. [MMIO + CSR] Wire carries values, not write history

"Never written" and "explicitly wrote the default value" look identical
in the drained file.

- Example: program writes `mcache_ctl=0` (disable caches) vs never
  touching it -- same drained bytes on a caches-off QEMU default.
- Solution: write-mask records the FACT at the source (translate-time
  CSR-write decode in the plugin); consumers never guess.

## 3. [MMIO vs CSR] Restore safety differs: CSR tolerant vs MMIO faulting

A CSR write to an unimplemented CSR is a tolerant no-op (cmderr
cleared); a Program-Buffer store to an absent MMIO region FAULTS.

- Example: `sw` to 0xE0500008 on an engine built with
  `NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB=0` -> PB fault.
- Solution: CSRs use tolerant writes + caps gating; MMIO restore is
  HARD-gated on hardware presence (`Simulator::l2c_present()`).

## 4. [MMIO] Side-effecting registers must never be written back

Restore is not "write everything back".

- Example: L2C CCTL Command register -- writing it RE-ISSUES a cache
  flush/invalidate; W1C error registers clear state on write.
- Solution: capture the FULL window for the record; restore only the
  boot-static writable whitelist (Control, HPM Control, Way Masks).

## 5. [MMIO + CSR] Hardware-driven values cannot be verified

Functional and cycle clocks legitimately diverge.

- Example: `mip` timer bit, `mcycle`/`minstret`, `mhpmcounter3-6`,
  L2C `INITSTATUS[14]`.
- Solution: verify exclusion list / bit masks -- not transport bugs.

## 6. [MMIO + CSR] Access rules differ per register class

Each class has one legal transport method.

- Example: L2C requires <8-byte accesses (DS220 11.8.3) -> `sw`/`lwu`,
  never `sd`/`ld`; `vtype`/`vl` are only restorable via `vsetvl`
  (Tier B); CSR restore is one abstract command per CSR (a batched
  csrrw sweep cannot tolerate a mid-batch fault).
- Solution: dedicated path per class (PB word store, abstract per-CSR,
  vsetvl staging).

## 7. [MMIO + CSR] Engine capability variance; QEMU must stay engine-agnostic

Never bake one engine's knowledge into QEMU -- hybrid pairs QEMU with
DIFFERENT engines.

- Example: M-only `ax45mpv_premium` lacks S-mode CSRs and HSP; a future
  engine adds CLIC/Smstateen.
- Solution: caps/manifest gates live on the CONSUMER side (probe:
  "measure, don't model"); the driver owns the pairing (`-cpu
  andes-ax66`, `vlen=512`). QEMU keeps only spec constants.

## 8. [CSR] WARL pinning / legalization divergence

A restore write may not take; the two sides may legalize differently.

- Example: `dcsr.prv` WARL-pinned to 3 on an M-only engine; `mnvec`
  held at the reset vector by the RTL.
- Solution: write-then-read-back verification (prv mismatch aborts with
  a pick-an-S/U-engine error) or verify exclusion.

## 9. [CSR] QEMU-phase read-path infidelity

The guest READS config on QEMU and takes a branch; if QEMU's config
differs from the engine's, the wrong path already executed -- NO
transport policy can fix this.

- Example: BSP reads `mmsc_cfg.PPMA` to decide whether to program PMA.
- Solution: `-cpu` family pairing + per-knob properties (`vlen=512` is
  the precedent); add knobs as needed.

## 10. [MMIO] Devices that exist on only one side

MMIO regions vsim does not model fault when touched in the ROI.

- Example: PLIC, PIT, WDT, RTC, GPIO... absent from vsim's memory map.
- Solution: ROI contract -- do not touch them; inside the ROI use only
  dual-modeled devices (UART2, SimControl/HTIF).

## One-line summary

CSRs travel via "caps + write-mask + tolerant write"; MMIO travels via
"full-window capture + whitelist restore + hardware-presence gate";
verify masks hardware-driven values; engine knowledge stays in the
consumer/driver, QEMU keeps only spec constants.

# Hybrid State Transport: the 10 Problems, Explained

## Background (read this first)

A hybrid run uses TWO simulators for ONE program:

```
  QEMU (fast, no timing)          vsim (slow, cycle-accurate)
  boot + setup code       ---->   the measured region (ROI)
                        "handoff"
```

At the handoff we must make vsim's CPU look EXACTLY like QEMU's CPU at
that moment. This copy has two steps:

- **drain**: read all state out of QEMU into a file (`hybrid_state_v1`).
- **restore**: write that file into the vsim hart through the Debug
  Module, then let it run.

Two kinds of state travel:

- **CSR**: a register inside the CPU (mstatus, mcache_ctl, ...).
  Written by the `csrw` instruction.
- **MMIO**: a register inside a device, reached by a memory address
  (the L2 cache controller at 0xE0500000, ...). Written by a normal
  store instruction.

Everything below is a way this copy can silently go wrong.

---

## 1. [MMIO + CSR] QEMU and the engine wake up with different values

**What happens.** Most registers are never touched by the program; they
just keep their power-on ("reset") value. QEMU and the real RTL do not
always agree on that power-on value. The drain reads a value out of
QEMU, but it cannot know whether the program PUT it there or it is just
QEMU's default. So restore may overwrite the engine's correct default
with QEMU's wrong one.

**Step-by-step example (L2C CEN, the case we hit).**
1. Real chip: after reset, L2C Control bit CEN = 1 (L2 cache ON).
2. QEMU models the L2C block as plain RAM, so it reads 0.
3. The program trusts the hardware default and never writes it.
4. Drain reads CEN=0. Restore writes CEN=0 into vsim.
5. vsim runs the ROI with L2 OFF. Cycle count is several times too
   big. No error is printed anywhere.

CSR example: `mnvec`. QEMU resets it to 0; the Andes RTL resets it to
the hart's reset vector. (We know engine reset values only one way: the
`--probe` reads the freshly-reset hart; results are in each engine's
`csr_manifest.csv`. Never trust memory or hearsay -- `msp_bound` was
long quoted as "RTL resets 0", and the probe showed that was wrong.)

**Fix.** Two halves. (a) Values fixed by the IP spec: make QEMU boot
with the correct value -- we seed CEN=1 into the RAM stub at machine
init. (b) Values that differ per engine: do not copy untouched
registers at all -- see problem 2.

---

## 2. [MMIO + CSR] The file carries values, but not "who wrote them"

**What happens.** The drained file is just numbers. The same number can
mean two different things:

- (a) the program never touched the register (number = QEMU default);
- (b) the program deliberately wrote that number.

The right action is different: for (a) do NOT restore (let the engine
keep its own default); for (b) DO restore. But the consumer cannot tell
(a) from (b) by looking at the value.

**Example.** `mcache_ctl = 0` can mean "program disabled the caches on
purpose" or "program never touched it". Same bytes in the file.

**Fix (v6 write-mask).** Record the fact at the source, where it is
still known. The QEMU plugin decodes every CSR-write instruction at
translation time and sets one bit per register: "the guest wrote this".
Restore and verify then act only on registers whose bit is set. Cost is
near zero: only real CSR-write instructions get a callback, and those
run a handful of times during boot.

---

## 3. [MMIO vs CSR] A wrong CSR write is forgiven; a wrong MMIO write crashes

**What happens.** Restore pushes values into the halted hart through
the Debug Module. The failure mode differs by kind:

- CSR: writing a CSR this engine does not implement raises a small
  error flag (cmderr). We clear it and continue. Harmless.
- MMIO: storing to an address where this engine has NO device is a bus
  error. The Program Buffer faults and the whole resume aborts.

**Example.** Every current engine is built `NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB=0`
(no L2C device). A `sw` to 0xE0500008 on such an engine does not get
ignored -- it faults.

**Fix.** CSRs may use "try and forgive" (tolerant write + capability
list). MMIO must ask FIRST: "does this engine physically have the
device?" -- a hard gate read from the engine's build config
(`Simulator::l2c_present()`), no store issued when absent.

---

## 4. [MMIO] Some registers DO something when written

**What happens.** "Restore" means "write the drained values back". But
some registers are not storage -- they are buttons. Writing them
triggers an action, so writing back the drained value re-triggers the
action at ROI entry.

**Examples.**
- L2C CCTL Command register: writing 0x12 STARTS a full L2 flush.
  Blindly restoring it would run a cache flush inside the measured
  window -- wrong cycles.
- W1C error bits ("write 1 to clear"): writing the drained value back
  ERASES the error state instead of restoring it.
- Read-only Configuration register: the write is ignored anyway.

**Fix.** Capture the WHOLE window into the file (for the record and
for verify), but write back only a whitelist of plain-storage config:
Control, HPM Control, Way Allocation Masks.

---

## 5. [MMIO + CSR] Some values change by themselves

**What happens.** Timers tick and counters count, driven by hardware,
not by the program. QEMU advances by instructions, vsim by cycles, so
these values can NEVER match between the two sides -- even when the
transport is perfect. If `--verify` compared them, every single run
would fail with a false alarm.

**Examples.** `mip` timer-pending bit, `mcycle`/`minstret`,
`mhpmcounter3-6`, L2C `INITSTATUS[14]`.

**Fix.** Verify skips these fields (or masks single bits, like
INITSTATUS inside the L2C Control compare). This is physics, not a bug.

---

## 6. [MMIO + CSR] Each register class has its own legal access method

**What happens.** There is no universal "write register" operation.
Hardware imposes rules, and breaking them gives UNPREDICTABLE results
or faults.

**Examples.**
- L2C spec (DS220 11.8.3): accesses must be smaller than 8 bytes. So
  the transport must use `sw`/`lwu` (32-bit), never `sd`/`ld` (64-bit).
- `vl`/`vtype` cannot be written directly at all; only the `vsetvl`
  instruction sets them (and it also clears vstart, forcing a strict
  restore ORDER).
- CSRs restore one-at-a-time: in a batched script, one faulting CSR
  kills the whole batch halfway, leaving the hart half-restored.

**Fix.** One dedicated path per class: Program-Buffer word stores for
L2C, `vsetvl` staging for V config, per-CSR abstract commands for CSRs.

---

## 7. [MMIO + CSR] Many engines, one QEMU

**What happens.** Hybrid pairs the SAME QEMU with different vsim
engines (premium, ax46, future cores). Engines differ in which
registers even exist (HSP? CLIC? L2C?). If we hardcode one engine's
details into QEMU, every other engine silently gets the wrong behavior.

**Example.** `msp_bound` exists on ax46 (HSP) but not on premium.
A future engine adds CLIC CSRs that today's engines lack.

**Fix.** Engine knowledge lives on the CONSUMER side, measured per
engine: `--probe` reads the freshly-reset hart once and records which
CSRs exist and their reset values (`csr_manifest.csv` -- "measure,
don't model"). Restore/drain/verify consult that manifest. QEMU keeps
only family-level constants (`-cpu andes-ax66`, `vlen=512`).

---

## 8. [CSR] The hardware may silently refuse the write (WARL)

**What happens.** RISC-V lets a field accept only values it supports
("WARL": write any, read legal). You write X; the hardware keeps Y. The
Debug Module reports success, but the value is not there. Restore
"worked" and still did nothing.

**Examples.**
- `dcsr.prv` on an M-only engine is pinned to 3. Restoring a state
  whose privilege is U(0) does not take -- the ROI would run in the
  WRONG privilege mode.
- `mnvec` is WARL-held at the reset vector; a restore write of 0 is
  discarded.

**Fix.** For fields where it matters, write THEN read back and compare.
A `dcsr.prv` mismatch aborts the run with "this engine cannot run S/U
-- pick an S/U-capable engine". Fields that are only cosmetic go on the
verify exclusion list.

---

## 9. [CSR, MMIO reads too] The damage may already be done before the handoff

**What happens.** Transport copies state AT the boundary. But the boot
code already RAN on QEMU. If it READ a config register and took a
branch, and QEMU's config differs from the engine's, the wrong branch
already executed. No state copy can undo a branch.

**Step-by-step example.**
1. BSP boot code reads `mmsc_cfg.PPMA` ("do I have programmable PMA?").
2. The engine has PPMA=1, but QEMU's CPU model says 0.
3. The boot code SKIPS the PMA setup -- on QEMU, where it ran.
4. The drained state has unprogrammed PMA. vsim faithfully restores
   it. The ROI runs with memory attributes the real chip would never
   have.

MMIO variant: reading the L2C Configuration register's SIZE field
returns 0 from QEMU's RAM stub.

**Fix.** This is the one class transport can NEVER fix. The fix is
making QEMU's visible config match the engine family: the driver picks
`-cpu` per engine and passes properties (`vlen=512` is the existing
precedent). Add a property when a real case appears.

---

## 10. [MMIO] Devices that exist on only one side

**What happens.** QEMU models the whole AE350 platform (PLIC, PIT,
WDT, RTC, GPIO...). vsim models almost none of it -- only RAM, UART2,
SimControl/HTIF, and the debug module. Code inside the ROI that touches
a QEMU-only device runs fine in the functional phase and BUS-FAULTS in
the cycle phase.

**Example.** Reading the PIT timer inside the ROI.

**Fix.** A contract, not code: ROI code must not touch single-sided
devices. Inside the ROI, use only dual-modeled devices (UART2 printf,
SimControl exit). Their configuration cannot be transported either --
device state lives inside each simulator.

---

## Quick reference

| # | Kind | Problem in one line | Fix in one line |
|---|------|---------------------|-----------------|
| 1 | both | power-on defaults differ | seed QEMU (spec constants) / write-mask (engine differences) |
| 2 | both | value does not say who wrote it | write-mask records writes at the source |
| 3 | contrast | absent CSR forgives, absent MMIO faults | tolerant writes vs hard presence gate |
| 4 | MMIO | some registers are buttons, not storage | capture all, restore whitelist only |
| 5 | both | timers/counters never match | verify skips/masks them |
| 6 | both | each class has one legal access method | dedicated path per class |
| 7 | both | engines differ; QEMU serves them all | probe + manifest on consumer side |
| 8 | CSR | WARL: write "succeeds", value refused | read back and check, or exclude |
| 9 | CSR+ | wrong branch already ran on QEMU | match QEMU config via -cpu/properties |
| 10 | MMIO | device exists on one side only | ROI contract: do not touch |

**One sentence:** CSRs travel with "caps + write-mask + tolerant
write"; MMIO travels with "full capture + whitelist restore + presence
gate"; verify masks hardware-driven values; engine knowledge stays in
the driver/consumer, QEMU keeps only spec constants.

-Each class has one legal transport method.

+- (b) the program deliberately wrote that number.
-- Example: L2C requires <8-byte accesses (DS220 11.8.3) -> `sw`/`lwu`,

-  (Tier B); CSR restore is one abstract command per CSR (a batched

+translation time and sets one bit per register: "the guest wrote this".

+- MMIO: storing to an address where this engine has NO device is a bus
+  error. The Program Buffer faults and the whole resume aborts.

+**Fix.** CSRs may use "try and forgive" (tolerant write + capability
+list). MMIO must ask FIRST: "does this engine physically have the
+device?" -- a hard gate read from the engine's build config
+(`Simulator::l2c_present()`), no store issued when absent.
-- Example: BSP reads `mmsc_cfg.PPMA` to decide whether to program PMA.
-  MMIO variant: reading the L2C Configuration Register's SIZE field
-  (read-only, derived by HW) returns 0 from QEMU's RAM stub.
-- Solution: `-cpu` family pairing + per-knob properties (`vlen=512` is
-  the precedent); add knobs as needed.
+## 4. [MMIO] Some registers DO something when written
+**What happens.** "Restore" means "write the drained values back". But
+some registers are not storage -- they are buttons. Writing them
+triggers an action, so writing back the drained value re-triggers the
+action at ROI entry.
+**Examples.**
+- L2C CCTL Command register: writing 0x12 STARTS a full L2 flush.
+  Blindly restoring it would run a cache flush inside the measured
+  window -- wrong cycles.
+- W1C error bits ("write 1 to clear"): writing the drained value back
+  ERASES the error state instead of restoring it.
+- Read-only Configuration register: the write is ignored anyway.
+**Fix.** Capture the WHOLE window into the file (for the record and
+for verify), but write back only a whitelist of plain-storage config:
+Control, HPM Control, Way Allocation Masks.
+## 5. [MMIO + CSR] Some values change by themselves
+**What happens.** Timers tick and counters count, driven by hardware,
+not by the program. QEMU advances by instructions, vsim by cycles, so
+these values can NEVER match between the two sides -- even when the
+transport is perfect. If `--verify` compared them, every single run
+would fail with a false alarm.
+**Examples.** `mip` timer-pending bit, `mcycle`/`minstret`,
+`mhpmcounter3-6`, L2C `INITSTATUS[14]`.
+**Fix.** Verify skips these fields (or masks single bits, like
+INITSTATUS inside the L2C Control compare). This is physics, not a bug.
+## 6. [MMIO + CSR] Each register class has its own legal access method
+**What happens.** There is no universal "write register" operation.
+Hardware imposes rules, and breaking them gives UNPREDICTABLE results
+or faults.
+**Examples.**
+- L2C spec (DS220 11.8.3): accesses must be smaller than 8 bytes. So
+  the transport must use `sw`/`lwu` (32-bit), never `sd`/`ld` (64-bit).
+- `vl`/`vtype` cannot be written directly at all; only the `vsetvl`
+  instruction sets them (and it also clears vstart, forcing a strict
+  restore ORDER).
+- CSRs restore one-at-a-time: in a batched script, one faulting CSR
+  kills the whole batch halfway, leaving the hart half-restored.
+**Fix.** One dedicated path per class: Program-Buffer word stores for
+L2C, `vsetvl` staging for V config, per-CSR abstract commands for CSRs.
+## 7. [MMIO + CSR] Many engines, one QEMU
+**What happens.** Hybrid pairs the SAME QEMU with different vsim
+engines (premium, ax46, future cores). Engines differ in which
+registers even exist (HSP? CLIC? L2C?). If we hardcode one engine's
+details into QEMU, every other engine silently gets the wrong behavior.
+**Example.** `msp_bound` exists on ax46 (HSP) but not on premium.
+A future engine adds CLIC CSRs that today's engines lack.
+**Fix.** Engine knowledge lives on the CONSUMER side, measured per
+engine: `--probe` reads the freshly-reset hart once and records which
+CSRs exist and their reset values (`csr_manifest.csv` -- "measure,
+don't model"). Restore/drain/verify consult that manifest. QEMU keeps
+only family-level constants (`-cpu andes-ax66`, `vlen=512`).
+## 8. [CSR] The hardware may silently refuse the write (WARL)
+**What happens.** RISC-V lets a field accept only values it supports
+("WARL": write any, read legal). You write X; the hardware keeps Y. The
+Debug Module reports success, but the value is not there. Restore
+"worked" and still did nothing.
+**Examples.**
+- `dcsr.prv` on an M-only engine is pinned to 3. Restoring a state
+  whose privilege is U(0) does not take -- the ROI would run in the
+  WRONG privilege mode.
+- `mnvec` is WARL-held at the reset vector; a restore write of 0 is
+  discarded.
+**Fix.** For fields where it matters, write THEN read back and compare.
+A `dcsr.prv` mismatch aborts the run with "this engine cannot run S/U
+-- pick an S/U-capable engine". Fields that are only cosmetic go on the
+verify exclusion list.
+## 9. [CSR, MMIO reads too] The damage may already be done before the handoff
+**What happens.** Transport copies state AT the boundary. But the boot
+code already RAN on QEMU. If it READ a config register and took a
+branch, and QEMU's config differs from the engine's, the wrong branch
+already executed. No state copy can undo a branch.
+**Step-by-step example.**
+1. BSP boot code reads `mmsc_cfg.PPMA` ("do I have programmable PMA?").
+2. The engine has PPMA=1, but QEMU's CPU model says 0.
+3. The boot code SKIPS the PMA setup -- on QEMU, where it ran.
+4. The drained state has unprogrammed PMA. vsim faithfully restores
+   it. The ROI runs with memory attributes the real chip would never
+   have.
+MMIO variant: reading the L2C Configuration register's SIZE field
+returns 0 from QEMU's RAM stub.
+**Fix.** This is the one class transport can NEVER fix. The fix is
+making QEMU's visible config match the engine family: the driver picks
+`-cpu` per engine and passes properties (`vlen=512` is the existing
+precedent). Add a property when a real case appears.
## 10. [MMIO] Devices that exist on only one side
-MMIO regions vsim does not model fault when touched in the ROI.
+**What happens.** QEMU models the whole AE350 platform (PLIC, PIT,
+WDT, RTC, GPIO...). vsim models almost none of it -- only RAM, UART2,
+SimControl/HTIF, and the debug module. Code inside the ROI that touches
+a QEMU-only device runs fine in the functional phase and BUS-FAULTS in
+the cycle phase.
-- Example: PLIC, PIT, WDT, RTC, GPIO... absent from vsim's memory map.
-- Solution: ROI contract -- do not touch them; inside the ROI use only
-  dual-modeled devices (UART2, SimControl/HTIF).
+**Example.** Reading the PIT timer inside the ROI.
-## One-line summary
+**Fix.** A contract, not code: ROI code must not touch single-sided
+devices. Inside the ROI, use only dual-modeled devices (UART2 printf,
+SimControl exit). Their configuration cannot be transported either --
+device state lives inside each simulator.
-CSRs travel via "caps + write-mask + tolerant write"; MMIO travels via
-"full-window capture + whitelist restore + hardware-presence gate";
-verify masks hardware-driven values; engine knowledge stays in the
-consumer/driver, QEMU keeps only spec constants.
+## Quick reference
+| # | Kind | Problem in one line | Fix in one line |
+| 1 | both | power-on defaults differ | seed QEMU (spec constants) / write-mask (engine differences) |
+| 2 | both | value does not say who wrote it | write-mask records writes at the source |
+| 3 | contrast | absent CSR forgives, absent MMIO faults | tolerant writes vs hard presence gate |
+| 4 | MMIO | some registers are buttons, not storage | capture all, restore whitelist only |
+| 5 | both | timers/counters never match | verify skips/masks them |
+| 6 | both | each class has one legal access method | dedicated path per class |
+| 7 | both | engines differ; QEMU serves them all | probe + manifest on consumer side |
+| 8 | CSR | WARL: write "succeeds", value refused | read back and check, or exclude |
+| 9 | CSR+ | wrong branch already ran on QEMU | match QEMU config via -cpu/properties |
+| 10 | MMIO | device exists on one side only | ROI contract: do not touch |
+**One sentence:** CSRs travel with "caps + write-mask + tolerant
+write"; MMIO travels with "full capture + whitelist restore + presence
+gate"; verify masks hardware-driven values; engine knowledge stays in
+the driver/consumer, QEMU keeps only spec constants.

# Hybrid State Transport: Problem Checklist (MMIO + CSR)

The 10 problem classes we must solve when transporting MMIO / CSR state
between QEMU (functional producer) and a vsim engine (cycle consumer),
each with one example and the current solution.

## 1. [MMIO + CSR] Reset default divergence

An untouched register drains the PRODUCER's default, not the engine's
reset value.

- Example: L2C `CEN` -- QEMU's RAM stub reads 0, real HW resets to 1.
  `mnvec` -- QEMU resets 0, the Andes RTL resets it to the hart's reset
  vector (seen live in --verify on both engines).
- Solution: spec/IP-level constants -> seed QEMU (`CEN=1` at machine
  init). Engine-level differences -> v6 write-mask.
- How reset values are KNOWN at all: the `--probe` (halt the
  freshly-reset hart, read every CSR) -> each engine's
  csr_manifest.csv. Measured, never assumed. Cautionary tale:
  `msp_bound` was long quoted as "QEMU all-ones vs RTL 0", but the
  probe shows the HSP-capable ax46 ALSO resets all-ones -- the
  premium's "0" was an unimplemented-CSR artifact (a capability gap,
  class #7, not reset divergence).

## 2. [MMIO + CSR] Wire carries values, not write history

"Never written" and "explicitly wrote the default value" look identical
in the drained file.

- Example: program writes `mcache_ctl=0` (disable caches) vs never
  touching it -- same drained bytes on a caches-off QEMU default.
- Solution: write-mask records the FACT at the source (translate-time
  CSR-write decode in the plugin); consumers never guess.

## 3. [MMIO vs CSR] Restore safety differs: CSR tolerant vs MMIO faulting

A CSR write to an unimplemented CSR is a tolerant no-op (cmderr
cleared); a Program-Buffer store to an absent MMIO region FAULTS.

- Example: `sw` to 0xE0500008 on an engine built with
  `NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB=0` -> PB fault.
- Solution: CSRs use tolerant writes + caps gating; MMIO restore is
  HARD-gated on hardware presence (`Simulator::l2c_present()`).

## 4. [MMIO] Side-effecting registers must never be written back

Restore is not "write everything back".

- Example: L2C CCTL Command register -- writing it RE-ISSUES a cache
  flush/invalidate; W1C error registers clear state on write.
- Solution: capture the FULL window for the record; restore only the
  boot-static writable whitelist (Control, HPM Control, Way Masks).

## 5. [MMIO + CSR] Hardware-driven values cannot be verified

Functional and cycle clocks legitimately diverge.

- Example: `mip` timer bit, `mcycle`/`minstret`, `mhpmcounter3-6`,
  L2C `INITSTATUS[14]`.
- Solution: verify exclusion list / bit masks -- not transport bugs.

## 6. [MMIO + CSR] Access rules differ per register class

Each class has one legal transport method.

- Example: L2C requires <8-byte accesses (DS220 11.8.3) -> `sw`/`lwu`,
  never `sd`/`ld`; `vtype`/`vl` are only restorable via `vsetvl`
  (Tier B); CSR restore is one abstract command per CSR (a batched
  csrrw sweep cannot tolerate a mid-batch fault).
- Solution: dedicated path per class (PB word store, abstract per-CSR,
  vsetvl staging).

## 7. [MMIO + CSR] Engine capability variance; QEMU must stay engine-agnostic

Never bake one engine's knowledge into QEMU -- hybrid pairs QEMU with
DIFFERENT engines.

- Example: M-only `ax45mpv_premium` lacks S-mode CSRs and HSP; a future
  engine adds CLIC/Smstateen.
- Solution: caps/manifest gates live on the CONSUMER side (probe:
  "measure, don't model"); the driver owns the pairing (`-cpu
  andes-ax66`, `vlen=512`). QEMU keeps only spec constants.

## 8. [CSR] WARL pinning / legalization divergence

A restore write may not take; the two sides may legalize differently.

- Example: `dcsr.prv` WARL-pinned to 3 on an M-only engine; `mnvec`
  held at the reset vector by the RTL.
- Solution: write-then-read-back verification (prv mismatch aborts with
  a pick-an-S/U-engine error) or verify exclusion.

## 9. [CSR, MMIO reads too] QEMU-phase read-path infidelity

The guest READS config on QEMU and takes a branch; if QEMU's config
differs from the engine's, the wrong path already executed -- NO
transport policy can fix this.

- Example: BSP reads `mmsc_cfg.PPMA` to decide whether to program PMA.
  MMIO variant: reading the L2C Configuration Register's SIZE field
  (read-only, derived by HW) returns 0 from QEMU's RAM stub.
- Solution: `-cpu` family pairing + per-knob properties (`vlen=512` is
  the precedent); add knobs as needed.

## 10. [MMIO] Devices that exist on only one side

MMIO regions vsim does not model fault when touched in the ROI.

- Example: PLIC, PIT, WDT, RTC, GPIO... absent from vsim's memory map.
- Solution: ROI contract -- do not touch them; inside the ROI use only
  dual-modeled devices (UART2, SimControl/HTIF).

## One-line summary

CSRs travel via "caps + write-mask + tolerant write"; MMIO travels via
"full-window capture + whitelist restore + hardware-presence gate";
verify masks hardware-driven values; engine knowledge stays in the
consumer/driver, QEMU keeps only spec constants.

# Hybrid State Transport: CSR Problems and MMIO Problems

## Background (read this first)

A hybrid run uses TWO simulators for ONE program:

```
  QEMU (fast, no timing)          vsim (slow, cycle-accurate)
  boot + setup code       ---->   the measured region (ROI)
                        "handoff"
```

At the handoff we must make vsim's CPU look EXACTLY like QEMU's CPU at
that moment. The copy has two steps:

- **drain**: read all state out of QEMU into a file (`hybrid_state_v1`).
- **restore**: write that file into the vsim hart through the Debug
  Module, then let it run.

Two kinds of state travel, and their problems are different enough to
list separately:

- **CSR**: a register inside the CPU (mstatus, mcache_ctl, ...),
  accessed by the `csrr`/`csrw` instructions.
- **MMIO**: a register inside a device, reached by a memory address
  (the L2 cache controller at 0xE0500000, ...), accessed by ordinary
  load/store instructions.

---

# Part 1: CSR problems

## C1. QEMU and the engine wake up with different CSR values

**What happens.** A CSR the program never writes just keeps its
power-on ("reset") value. QEMU's reset value and the engine RTL's reset
value are not always the same. The drain cannot tell "program set this"
from "this is just QEMU's default", so restore may overwrite the
engine's correct default with QEMU's wrong one.

**Example.** `mnvec`: QEMU resets it to 0; the Andes RTL resets it to
the hart's reset vector. Seen live as a false `--verify` failure.

How engine reset values are KNOWN at all: only by measurement -- the
`--probe` halts the freshly-reset hart and reads every CSR, into each
engine's `csr_manifest.csv`. Never trust hearsay: `msp_bound` was long
quoted as "RTL resets 0", and the probe showed the HSP-capable ax46
also resets all-ones, same as QEMU.

**Fix.** Do not transport what the program never wrote -> C2.

## C2. A drained value does not say who wrote it

**What happens.** The drained file is just numbers. `mcache_ctl = 0`
can mean "program disabled the caches on purpose" or "program never
touched it and 0 is QEMU's default". The right action differs:
deliberate write -> restore it; untouched -> keep the engine's own

Module reports success, so restore "worked" but the value is not there.

a U-mode state does not take, and the ROI would run in the wrong
privilege. `mnvec` is held at the reset vector; a restored 0 is

not the program. QEMU advances by instructions, vsim by cycles, so

which starts as all zeros. The real device has spec-defined reset
values. A program that trusts the hardware default never writes the
register, so the drain reads QEMU's zero -- and restore would push that

2. QEMU's RAM stub reads 0.

   no error is printed anywhere.

constant, not an engine choice -- and once defaults agree, the
"untouched vs wrote-the-default" ambiguity (C2's problem) becomes
harmless for MMIO too.

**What happens.** MMIO restore is a store instruction executed by the
halted hart (through the Program Buffer). If this engine was built
WITHOUT the device, there is nothing at that address: the store is a
bus error, the Program Buffer faults, and the whole resume aborts.

own build config (`_NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB > 0`, `_NDS_L2C_REG_BASE`)

destroys state, so "write the drained value back" is wrong for them.

**Examples.** L2C CCTL Command register: writing 0x12 STARTS a full L2
flush -- restoring it would run a cache flush inside the measured
window. W1C error bits: writing 1 CLEARS them, so writing the drained
value back erases the error state. The Configuration register is
read-only anyway.

verify), but write back only a whitelist of plain-storage config:
Control, HPM Control, Way Allocation Masks. (Mirror: C6.)

cannot match between a functional model and a cycle model.

**Example.** L2C `INITSTATUS[14]`: a real L2C drives it while its TAG
RAMs initialize; QEMU's RAM stub never changes it.

**Fix.** `--verify` masks the bit out of the Control-register compare.
(Mirror: C5.)

## M5. The device dictates the access width

**What happens.** Device buses have rules; breaking them is
UNPREDICTABLE per the spec.

**Example.** DS220 11.8.3: L2C registers must be accessed with single
transfers SMALLER than 8 bytes. So the transport must use `sw`/`lwu`
(32-bit), never `sd`/`ld` (64-bit), even though the registers are

`encode_lwu`); `lwu` (zero-extend) so a 32-bit read does not
sign-pollute the 64-bit slot. (Mirror: C7.)

QEMU's RAM stub returns whatever is in RAM (mostly zeros), not what the
real device would report -- and the wrong branch has already run by the
time we hand off.

a real workload needs it.

## M7. Devices that exist on only one side

**What happens.** QEMU models the whole AE350 platform (PLIC, PIT,
WDT, RTC, GPIO, DMAC...). vsim models only a handful (its
`platform/memory_map.h`): RAM, local memories (ILM/DLM), UART1/2,
SimControl, the debug module, SMU, the AIA interrupt files -- no PLIC,
no timers, no GPIO. ROI code touching a QEMU-only device runs fine in
the functional phase and BUS-FAULTS in the cycle phase. Their internal
state also cannot be transported -- it lives inside each simulator.

devices; inside the ROI use only dual-modeled ones (UART2 printf,

|-----|---------|-----|

| C2 | value has no write-history (mcache_ctl=0) | write-mask, recorded at source |
| C3 | CSR absent on this engine (msp_bound) | tolerant write + probe/manifest caps |
| C4 | WARL silently refuses (dcsr.prv) | read back + abort, or exclude |
| C5 | hardware-driven (mip, mcycle) | verify skips |
| C6 | action CSRs (mcctlcommand) | never in the transported list |
| C7 | special write methods (vl/vtype) | vsetvl staging, per-CSR, ordering |
| C8 | wrong branch already ran (mmsc_cfg.PPMA) | -cpu / properties (vlen=512) |

| MMIO | Problem | Fix |
|------|---------|-----|
| M1 | stub wakes up wrong (CEN=0) | seed spec reset at machine init |
| M2 | absent device faults the restore | hard presence gate from build config |
| M3 | button registers (CCTL, W1C) | capture all, restore whitelist |
| M4 | self-changing status (INITSTATUS) | verify bit-mask |
| M5 | access-width rules (<8 bytes) | sw/lwu word transport |
| M6 | stub lies to readers (Config SIZE) | seed what's knowable; model on demand |
| M7 | single-sided devices (PLIC, PIT) | ROI contract: don't touch |

**Shared principles.** Engine knowledge stays in the consumer/driver

masks values driven by hardware clocks; and state that the program
never wrote is the engine's business, not the producer's.

-**Fix.** Two halves. (a) Values fixed by the IP spec: make QEMU boot
-with the correct value -- we seed CEN=1 into the RAM stub at machine
-init. (b) Values that differ per engine: do not copy untouched
-registers at all -- see problem 2.
+How engine reset values are KNOWN at all: only by measurement -- the
+`--probe` halts the freshly-reset hart and reads every CSR, into each
+engine's `csr_manifest.csv`. Never trust hearsay: `msp_bound` was long
+quoted as "RTL resets 0", and the probe showed the HSP-capable ax46
+also resets all-ones, same as QEMU.
+**Fix.** Do not transport what the program never wrote -> C2.
-## 2. [MMIO + CSR] The file carries values, but not "who wrote them"
+## C2. A drained value does not say who wrote it
-**What happens.** The drained file is just numbers. The same number can
-mean two different things:
+**What happens.** The drained file is just numbers. `mcache_ctl = 0`
+can mean "program disabled the caches on purpose" or "program never
+touched it and 0 is QEMU's default". The right action differs:
+deliberate write -> restore it; untouched -> keep the engine's own
+default. The consumer cannot tell the two apart from the value.
-- (a) the program never touched the register (number = QEMU default);
-- (b) the program deliberately wrote that number.
+**Fix (v6 write-mask).** Record the fact at the source, where it is
+still known: the QEMU plugin decodes every CSR-write instruction at
+translation time (`csrrw`/`csrrwi` always write; `csrrs/c` only when
+rs1 != x0; `csrrsi/ci` only when uimm != 0) and sets one bit per
+governed CSR. Restore and `--verify` act only on set bits. Together
+with C1 this makes reset divergence harmless for every engine, with no
+per-engine data inside QEMU.
-The right action is different: for (a) do NOT restore (let the engine
-keep its own default); for (b) DO restore. But the consumer cannot tell
-(a) from (b) by looking at the value.
+## C3. This engine may not implement the CSR at all
-**Example.** `mcache_ctl = 0` can mean "program disabled the caches on
-purpose" or "program never touched it". Same bytes in the file.
+**What happens.** Engines differ in which CSRs even exist: premium has
+no HSP (`msp_bound` absent), ax46 has it; a future engine adds CLIC.
+One QEMU must serve them all, so nothing engine-specific may be
+hardcoded into QEMU, and the restore must not assume a CSR exists.
-**Fix (v6 write-mask).** Record the fact at the source, where it is
-still known. The QEMU plugin decodes every CSR-write instruction at
-translation time and sets one bit per register: "the guest wrote this".
-Restore and verify then act only on registers whose bit is set. Cost is
-near zero: only real CSR-write instructions get a callback, and those
-run a handful of times during boot.
+**Example.** Restoring `msp_bound` on premium: the CSR is not there.
+**Fix.** Two layers on the CONSUMER side. (a) A write to an absent CSR
+raises a small error flag (cmderr) that we clear and continue --
+"tolerant write", so nothing breaks. (b) The per-engine capability
+manifest (from the same `--probe`; "measure, don't model") gates
+restore/drain/verify so absent CSRs are skipped, not attempted. QEMU
+keeps only family-level constants (`-cpu andes-ax66`, `vlen=512`).
+(Mirror on the MMIO side: M2 -- there the wrong access FAULTS.)
-## 3. [MMIO vs CSR] A wrong CSR write is forgiven; a wrong MMIO write crashes
+## C4. The hardware may silently refuse the write (WARL)
-**What happens.** Restore pushes values into the halted hart through
-the Debug Module. The failure mode differs by kind:
+**What happens.** A RISC-V field may accept only values it supports
+("write any, read legal"). You write X, the hardware keeps Y. The Debug
+Module reports success, so restore "worked" but the value is not there.
-- CSR: writing a CSR this engine does not implement raises a small
-  error flag (cmderr). We clear it and continue. Harmless.
-- MMIO: storing to an address where this engine has NO device is a bus
-  error. The Program Buffer faults and the whole resume aborts.
+**Examples.** `dcsr.prv` on an M-only engine is pinned to 3: restoring
+a U-mode state does not take, and the ROI would run in the wrong
+privilege. `mnvec` is held at the reset vector; a restored 0 is
+discarded.
-**Example.** Every current engine is built `NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB=0`
-(no L2C device). A `sw` to 0xE0500008 on such an engine does not get
-ignored -- it faults.
+**Fix.** Where it matters, write THEN read back and compare:
+a `dcsr.prv` mismatch aborts with "pick an S/U-capable engine".
+Cosmetic cases go on the verify exclusion list.
-**Fix.** CSRs may use "try and forgive" (tolerant write + capability
-list). MMIO must ask FIRST: "does this engine physically have the
-device?" -- a hard gate read from the engine's build config
-(`Simulator::l2c_present()`), no store issued when absent.
+## C5. Some CSR values change by themselves
+**What happens.** Counters and pending bits are driven by hardware,
+not the program. QEMU advances by instructions, vsim by cycles, so
+these can NEVER match -- even when the transport is perfect. Comparing
+them would fail every run with a false alarm.
-## 4. [MMIO] Some registers DO something when written
+**Examples.** `mip` timer-pending bit, `mcycle`/`minstret`,
+`mhpmcounter3-6`.
-**What happens.** "Restore" means "write the drained values back". But
-some registers are not storage -- they are buttons. Writing them
-triggers an action, so writing back the drained value re-triggers the
-action at ROI entry.
+**Fix.** `--verify` skips them. Physics, not a bug.
-**Examples.**
-- L2C CCTL Command register: writing 0x12 STARTS a full L2 flush.
-  Blindly restoring it would run a cache flush inside the measured
-  window -- wrong cycles.
-- W1C error bits ("write 1 to clear"): writing the drained value back
-  ERASES the error state instead of restoring it.
-- Read-only Configuration register: the write is ignored anyway.
+## C6. Action CSRs must not be transported at all
-**Fix.** Capture the WHOLE window into the file (for the record and
-for verify), but write back only a whitelist of plain-storage config:
-Control, HPM Control, Way Allocation Masks.
+**What happens.** Some CSRs are commands, not storage: writing them
+performs an operation. Restoring a drained command value would re-run
+the operation at ROI entry.
+**Example.** `mcctlcommand` (0x7CC) issues an L1 cache operation on
+write. It is deliberately ABSENT from the transported M-ext list, while
+its neighbors `mcctlbeginaddr`/`mcctldata` (plain storage) are in.
-## 5. [MMIO + CSR] Some values change by themselves
+**Fix.** The transported CSR list contains only registers that are
+plain state -- readable and writable with no side effects. (Mirror on
+the MMIO side: M3.)
-**What happens.** Timers tick and counters count, driven by hardware,
-not by the program. QEMU advances by instructions, vsim by cycles, so
-these values can NEVER match between the two sides -- even when the
-transport is perfect. If `--verify` compared them, every single run
-would fail with a false alarm.
+## C7. Each CSR has its own legal write method
-**Examples.** `mip` timer-pending bit, `mcycle`/`minstret`,
-`mhpmcounter3-6`, L2C `INITSTATUS[14]`.
+**What happens.** Not every CSR can be written directly, and the order
+of writes matters.
-**Fix.** Verify skips these fields (or masks single bits, like
-INITSTATUS inside the L2C Control compare). This is physics, not a bug.
+**Examples.** `vl`/`vtype` cannot be written by `csrw` at all -- only
+the `vsetvl` instruction sets them, and `vsetvl` also clears `vstart`,
+so `vstart` must be restored AFTER it. A batched restore script dies
+halfway if one CSR faults, leaving the hart half-restored -- so CSRs
+restore one abstract command at a time.
+**Fix.** Dedicated paths: `vsetvl` staging for V config, strict restore
+ordering, per-CSR abstract commands (no batched restore).
-## 6. [MMIO + CSR] Each register class has its own legal access method
+## C8. The wrong branch already ran before the handoff
-**What happens.** There is no universal "write register" operation.
-Hardware imposes rules, and breaking them gives UNPREDICTABLE results
-or faults.
+**What happens.** Transport copies state AT the boundary, but the boot
+code already RAN on QEMU. If it READ a config CSR and QEMU's config
+differs from the engine's, it took the wrong branch -- and no state
+copy can undo a branch that already executed.
-**Examples.**
-- L2C spec (DS220 11.8.3): accesses must be smaller than 8 bytes. So
-  the transport must use `sw`/`lwu` (32-bit), never `sd`/`ld` (64-bit).
-- `vl`/`vtype` cannot be written directly at all; only the `vsetvl`
-  instruction sets them (and it also clears vstart, forcing a strict
-  restore ORDER).
-- CSRs restore one-at-a-time: in a batched script, one faulting CSR
-  kills the whole batch halfway, leaving the hart half-restored.
+**Step-by-step example.**
+1. BSP reads `mmsc_cfg.PPMA` ("do I have programmable PMA?").
+2. The engine has PPMA=1; QEMU's CPU model says 0.
+3. The boot code SKIPS the PMA setup -- on QEMU, where it ran.
+4. vsim faithfully restores a state with unprogrammed PMA. The ROI
+   runs with memory attributes the real chip would never have.
-**Fix.** One dedicated path per class: Program-Buffer word stores for
-L2C, `vsetvl` staging for V config, per-CSR abstract commands for CSRs.
+**Fix.** The one class transport can never fix. Make QEMU's VISIBLE
+config match the engine family: the driver picks `-cpu` per engine and
+passes properties (`vlen=512` is the precedent). Add a knob when a real
+case appears. (Mirror on the MMIO side: M6.)
-## 7. [MMIO + CSR] Many engines, one QEMU
+# Part 2: MMIO problems
-**What happens.** Hybrid pairs the SAME QEMU with different vsim
-engines (premium, ax46, future cores). Engines differ in which
-registers even exist (HSP? CLIC? L2C?). If we hardcode one engine's
-details into QEMU, every other engine silently gets the wrong behavior.
+## M1. The device model wakes up with the wrong values
-**Example.** `msp_bound` exists on ax46 (HSP) but not on premium.
-A future engine adds CLIC CSRs that today's engines lack.
+**What happens.** QEMU models the L2C register block as plain RAM,
+which starts as all zeros. The real device has spec-defined reset
+values. A program that trusts the hardware default never writes the
+register, so the drain reads QEMU's zero -- and restore would push that
+zero into a real device model.
-**Fix.** Engine knowledge lives on the CONSUMER side, measured per
-engine: `--probe` reads the freshly-reset hart once and records which
-CSRs exist and their reset values (`csr_manifest.csv` -- "measure,
-don't model"). Restore/drain/verify consult that manifest. QEMU keeps
-only family-level constants (`-cpu andes-ax66`, `vlen=512`).
+**Step-by-step example (L2C CEN, the case we hit).**
+1. Real chip: after reset, L2C Control bit CEN = 1 (L2 cache ON).
+2. QEMU's RAM stub reads 0.
+3. The program relies on the default and never writes it.
+4. Drain reads CEN=0; restore writes CEN=0 into vsim.
+5. The ROI runs with L2 OFF: cycle count several times too big, and
+   no error is printed anywhere.
+**Fix.** Seed the stub with the spec reset value at machine init (we
+store CEN=1). This is safe to hardcode because it is an IP-spec
+constant, not an engine choice -- and once defaults agree, the
+"untouched vs wrote-the-default" ambiguity (C2's problem) becomes
+harmless for MMIO too.
-## 8. [CSR] The hardware may silently refuse the write (WARL)
+## M2. Restoring into an absent device FAULTS
-**What happens.** RISC-V lets a field accept only values it supports
-("WARL": write any, read legal). You write X; the hardware keeps Y. The
-Debug Module reports success, but the value is not there. Restore
-"worked" and still did nothing.
+**What happens.** MMIO restore is a store instruction executed by the
+halted hart (through the Program Buffer). If this engine was built
+WITHOUT the device, there is nothing at that address: the store is a
+bus error, the Program Buffer faults, and the whole resume aborts.
+Unlike a CSR (C3), there is no "tolerant" mode for memory.
-**Examples.**
-- `dcsr.prv` on an M-only engine is pinned to 3. Restoring a state
-  whose privilege is U(0) does not take -- the ROI would run in the
-  WRONG privilege mode.
-- `mnvec` is WARL-held at the reset vector; a restore write of 0 is
-  discarded.
+**Example.** Every current engine is built `NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB=0`.
+A `sw` to 0xE0500008 on them does not get ignored -- it faults.
-**Fix.** For fields where it matters, write THEN read back and compare.
-A `dcsr.prv` mismatch aborts the run with "this engine cannot run S/U
--- pick an S/U-capable engine". Fields that are only cosmetic go on the
-verify exclusion list.
+**Fix.** A HARD presence gate before any store: the simulator asks its
+own build config (`_NDS_L2C_CACHE_SIZE_KB > 0`, `_NDS_L2C_REG_BASE`)
+and skips the whole L2C restore when the device is absent.
+## M3. Some device registers are buttons, not storage
-## 9. [CSR, MMIO reads too] The damage may already be done before the handoff
+**What happens.** Writing certain MMIO registers triggers an action or
+destroys state, so "write the drained value back" is wrong for them.
-**What happens.** Transport copies state AT the boundary. But the boot
-code already RAN on QEMU. If it READ a config register and took a
-branch, and QEMU's config differs from the engine's, the wrong branch
-already executed. No state copy can undo a branch.
+**Examples.** L2C CCTL Command register: writing 0x12 STARTS a full L2
+flush -- restoring it would run a cache flush inside the measured
+window. W1C error bits: writing 1 CLEARS them, so writing the drained
+value back erases the error state. The Configuration register is
+read-only anyway.
-**Step-by-step example.**
-1. BSP boot code reads `mmsc_cfg.PPMA` ("do I have programmable PMA?").
-2. The engine has PPMA=1, but QEMU's CPU model says 0.
-3. The boot code SKIPS the PMA setup -- on QEMU, where it ran.
-4. The drained state has unprogrammed PMA. vsim faithfully restores
-   it. The ROI runs with memory attributes the real chip would never
-   have.
+**Fix.** Capture the WHOLE window into the file (for the record and
+verify), but write back only a whitelist of plain-storage config:
+Control, HPM Control, Way Allocation Masks. (Mirror: C6.)
-MMIO variant: reading the L2C Configuration register's SIZE field
-returns 0 from QEMU's RAM stub.
+## M4. Some device status changes by itself
-**Fix.** This is the one class transport can NEVER fix. The fix is
-making QEMU's visible config match the engine family: the driver picks
-`-cpu` per engine and passes properties (`vlen=512` is the existing
-precedent). Add a property when a real case appears.
+**What happens.** Status bits driven by the device, not the program,
+cannot match between a functional model and a cycle model.
+**Example.** L2C `INITSTATUS[14]`: a real L2C drives it while its TAG
+RAMs initialize; QEMU's RAM stub never changes it.
-## 10. [MMIO] Devices that exist on only one side
+**Fix.** `--verify` masks the bit out of the Control-register compare.
+(Mirror: C5.)
+## M5. The device dictates the access width
+**What happens.** Device buses have rules; breaking them is
+UNPREDICTABLE per the spec.
+**Example.** DS220 11.8.3: L2C registers must be accessed with single
+transfers SMALLER than 8 bytes. So the transport must use `sw`/`lwu`
+(32-bit), never `sd`/`ld` (64-bit), even though the registers are
+64-bit-wide slots in the file.
+**Fix.** The restore/drain path encodes word accesses (`encode_sw`,
+`encode_lwu`); `lwu` (zero-extend) so a 32-bit read does not
+sign-pollute the 64-bit slot. (Mirror: C7.)
+## M6. The stub lies to programs that READ it
+**What happens.** Boot code may read device config and branch on it.
+QEMU's RAM stub returns whatever is in RAM (mostly zeros), not what the
+real device would report -- and the wrong branch has already run by the
+time we hand off.
+**Example.** Reading the L2C Configuration register's SIZE field
+returns 0 from the stub; boot code sizing its flush loop by it would
+misbehave.
+**Fix.** Same as C8: transport cannot fix reads that already happened.
+Seed the values QEMU can know (M1); model more of the device only when
+a real workload needs it.
+## M7. Devices that exist on only one side
**What happens.** QEMU models the whole AE350 platform (PLIC, PIT,
-WDT, RTC, GPIO, DMAC...). vsim models only a handful (see its
-`platform/memory_map.h`): RAM, the local memories (ILM/DLM), UART1/2,
-SimControl, the debug module, SMU, and the AIA interrupt files --
-no PLIC, no timers, no GPIO. Code inside the ROI that touches a
-QEMU-only device runs fine in the functional phase and BUS-FAULTS in
-the cycle phase.
+WDT, RTC, GPIO, DMAC...). vsim models only a handful (its
+`platform/memory_map.h`): RAM, local memories (ILM/DLM), UART1/2,
+SimControl, the debug module, SMU, the AIA interrupt files -- no PLIC,
+no timers, no GPIO. ROI code touching a QEMU-only device runs fine in
+the functional phase and BUS-FAULTS in the cycle phase. Their internal
+state also cannot be transported -- it lives inside each simulator.
**Example.** Reading the PIT timer inside the ROI.
-**Fix.** A contract, not code: ROI code must not touch single-sided
-devices. Inside the ROI, use only dual-modeled devices (UART2 printf,
-SimControl exit). Their configuration cannot be transported either --
-device state lives inside each simulator.
+**Fix.** A contract, not code: the ROI must not touch single-sided
+devices; inside the ROI use only dual-modeled ones (UART2 printf,
+SimControl exit).
-## Quick reference
+# Quick reference
-| # | Kind | Problem in one line | Fix in one line |
-| 1 | both | power-on defaults differ | seed QEMU (spec constants) / write-mask (engine differences) |
-| 2 | both | value does not say who wrote it | write-mask records writes at the source |
-| 3 | contrast | absent CSR forgives, absent MMIO faults | tolerant writes vs hard presence gate |
-| 4 | MMIO | some registers are buttons, not storage | capture all, restore whitelist only |
-| 5 | both | timers/counters never match | verify skips/masks them |
-| 6 | both | each class has one legal access method | dedicated path per class |
-| 7 | both | engines differ; QEMU serves them all | probe + manifest on consumer side |
-| 8 | CSR | WARL: write "succeeds", value refused | read back and check, or exclude |
-| 9 | CSR+ | wrong branch already ran on QEMU | match QEMU config via -cpu/properties |
-| 10 | MMIO | device exists on one side only | ROI contract: do not touch |
+| CSR | Problem | Fix |
+| C1 | reset defaults differ (mnvec) | don't transport unwritten -> C2 |
+| C2 | value has no write-history (mcache_ctl=0) | write-mask, recorded at source |
+| C3 | CSR absent on this engine (msp_bound) | tolerant write + probe/manifest caps |
+| C4 | WARL silently refuses (dcsr.prv) | read back + abort, or exclude |
+| C5 | hardware-driven (mip, mcycle) | verify skips |
+| C6 | action CSRs (mcctlcommand) | never in the transported list |
+| C7 | special write methods (vl/vtype) | vsetvl staging, per-CSR, ordering |
+| C8 | wrong branch already ran (mmsc_cfg.PPMA) | -cpu / properties (vlen=512) |
-**One sentence:** CSRs travel with "caps + write-mask + tolerant
-write"; MMIO travels with "full capture + whitelist restore + presence
-gate"; verify masks hardware-driven values; engine knowledge stays in
-the driver/consumer, QEMU keeps only spec constants.
+| MMIO | Problem | Fix |
+| M1 | stub wakes up wrong (CEN=0) | seed spec reset at machine init |
+| M2 | absent device faults the restore | hard presence gate from build config |
+| M3 | button registers (CCTL, W1C) | capture all, restore whitelist |
+| M4 | self-changing status (INITSTATUS) | verify bit-mask |
+| M5 | access-width rules (<8 bytes) | sw/lwu word transport |
+| M6 | stub lies to readers (Config SIZE) | seed what's knowable; model on demand |
+| M7 | single-sided devices (PLIC, PIT) | ROI contract: don't touch |
+**Shared principles.** Engine knowledge stays in the consumer/driver
+(probe -> manifest -> gates); QEMU keeps only spec constants; verify
+masks values driven by hardware clocks; and state that the program
+never wrote is the engine's business, not the producer's.
